text: The Lebedev Physical Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences (Russian: Физи́ческий институ́т имени П. Н. Ле́бедева Российской академии наук) is a Russian research institute located in Moscow, specializing in physics. It was established in its current form in 1934 by academician Sergey Vavilov and moved to Moscow that same year, being named after the Russian physicist Pyotr Lebedev. It is also known as the P. N. Lebedev Institute of Physics or simply the Lebedev Institute. In Russian, it is commonly referred to by the acronym FIAN (ФИАН), standing for "Physical Institute of the Academy of Sciences". The institute's research activities cover a wide range of fields, including laser technology, dark matter structure, nanostructures, superconductivity, cosmic rays, and gamma-astronomy. It developed a technique for crystallizing cubic zirconia, known in Russia as Fianit, named after FIAN. The institute operates a particle accelerator, a 1.2 GeV electron synchrotron called "Pakhra", located in Troitsk near Moscow at the LPI's HEP department. However, the institute is not entirely or primarily focused on accelerator or particle physics, as its research scope encompasses most areas of modern physics. The Andreyev Acoustics Institute is a part of the Lebedev Physical Institute and is named after Nikolay Andreyev. In 2021, a documentary titled "Mishik Kazaryan: The Path of an Explorer" (original title «Мишик Казарян: путь Искателя») was released, directed by Leonid Ioffe, and narrates the life and work of Professor Mishik Kazaryan, an experimental physicist and laureate of the USSR State Prize who worked at the Lebedev Physical Institute. The film provides insight into the daily life of the institute from the mid-1960s. The institute's geographical coordinates are 55°41′52″N 37°33′55″E (55.69778°N 37.56528°E).
